title: Hepatic haemangioma
subject: Medicine
summary: Benign vascular liver tumour, usually incidental. Small lesions need no treatment; larger or symptomatic lesions require careful assessment and possible intervention.

sections.p: A hepatic haemangioma is a benign collection of blood‑filled vascular channels in the liver. Diagnosis is radiological, based on characteristic imaging patterns.
b: Incidental finding on ultrasound or CT
Typical peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill‑in on contrast studies

sections.p: Most lesions are <5 cm and asymptomatic. Larger lesions (>5 cm) are termed “giant” and may cause symptoms or complications.
b: Small (<5 cm): observation only
Giant (≥5 cm): consider symptoms, growth, risk of rupture

sections.p: Exact aetiology is unknown; hormonal influences (estrogen) promote growth. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing liver disease (e.g., hepatitis B, schistosomiasis) may be present but does not cause haemangioma.
b: Estrogen exposure (pregnancy, oral contraceptives)
Congenital vascular malformation

sections.p: Usually asymptomatic. When symptomatic, patients report right upper quadrant fullness, vague abdominal pain, or early satiety.
b: Incidental lesion on imaging for another reason
Pain or discomfort if lesion is large

sections.p: If CT/MRI is unavailable, a contrast‑enhanced ultrasound (if portable) can be used; otherwise, monitor with serial ultrasound.

t.b: Is there a focal liver lesion? – Shows hyperechoic, well‑circumscribed mass; may need Doppler
What is the lesion’s vascular pattern? – Peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill‑in confirms haemangioma

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin)
t.b: Is there underlying liver disease? – Normal results support isolated benign lesion

t.a: Serology for hepatitis B/C, schistosomiasis (if endemic)
t.b: Is chronic liver disease present? – Positive tests prompt separate management

sections.p: Complications are rare but can be life‑threatening.
b: Rapid growth >1 cm/yr
Lesion >10 cm with pain
Rupture causing intra‑abdominal hemorrhage
Kasabach‑Merritt phenomenon (consumptive coagulopathy) – extremely rare

sections.p: Most lesions need no active treatment; focus on symptom control and avoiding unnecessary interventions.
b: Observation with ultrasound every 6–12 months for lesions ≥5 cm
Avoid biopsy – high risk of bleeding
If symptomatic or rapidly enlarging: consider selective trans‑arterial embolisation (TAE) or surgical resection
Pregnant women: counsel on possible growth but usually no intervention

sections.p: Regular imaging for larger lesions; educate patients on warning symptoms.
b: Ultrasound at 6 months, then yearly if stable
Advise to seek care for sudden abdominal pain or signs of shock

sections.p: Other focal liver lesions can mimic haemangioma on imaging.
b: Focal nodular hyperplasia – central scar, homogeneous arterial enhancement
Hepatocellular adenoma – arterial phase hyperenhancement, risk of rupture
Metastatic disease – irregular borders, variable enhancement

sections.p: Certain imaging features overlap with malignant lesions, especially in cirrhotic livers.
b: Small haemangiomas may appear iso‑attenuating on non‑contrast CT – risk of misclassification
Contrast timing errors can obscure peripheral nodular pattern

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension – possible rupture
Rapid increase in lesion size on serial imaging
New onset coagulopathy or unexplained thrombocytopenia

faq.q: Do all hepatic haemangiomas need treatment?
faq.a: No, >90 % are small and asymptomatic; observation is sufficient.
The vascular nature leads to a high risk of uncontrolled bleeding.

faq.q: Can oral contraceptives worsen a haemangioma?
faq.a: Estrogen can promote growth, so clinicians may advise switching to non‑estrogenic contraception if the lesion is large.

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman with a 6‑cm liver lesion on ultrasound asks about surgery – discuss indications for intervention and alternatives — answer should cover symptoms, growth, rupture risk, and TAE vs resection.

During a routine antenatal scan a 4‑cm haemangioma is seen – what advice do you give and what follow‑up is required? — emphasise observation, avoid biopsy, monitor for pain, counsel on estrogen effect.

A patient with chronic hepatitis B has a 3‑cm lesion that is hyperechoic on ultrasound – how do you differentiate haemangioma from early HCC? — describe imaging phases, need for contrast CT/MRI, and role of AFP.
You have only an ultrasound machine in a district hospital – how would you confirm a haemangioma? — explain characteristic sonographic features and when to refer for advanced imaging.

A child presents with a large abdominal mass and coagulopathy – why is Kasabach‑Merritt syndrome considered and how does it differ from a hepatic haemangioma? — outline consumptive coagulopathy and typical cutaneous lesions.
A patient on oral contraceptives develops new right‑upper‑quadrant pain – what investigations do you order and why? — list ultrasound, LFTs, and discuss hormonal influence.
During surgery for a presumed haemangioma, massive bleeding occurs – what pre‑operative steps could have prevented this? — stress avoidance of biopsy, use of imaging to confirm diagnosis.
Explain why a giant haemangioma (>10 cm) may cause early satiety – link lesion size to hepatic capsule stretch and reduced gastric capacity.
